title: Login — contract v1
description:
The request and response shapes of Dudo's login path, contract version 1. This file defines SHAPES ONLY. A type alone is not a contract: the normalisation rule, the client-side KDF parameters, the disclosure rulings, the reserved paths and the error conditions are in login-v1.contract.yaml and README.md in this directory, and all three are normative together.

THIS CONTRACT WAS WRITTEN AFTER THE IMPLEMENTATION IT DESCRIBES, AND THAT IS STATED HERE RATHER THAN ONLY IN THE PROSE. platform/core/identity/login.ts was built before any contract existed, out of order under .claude/rules/workflow.md §3, and two client agents then had to guess the field names from source — one of them guessed wrong. Every shape below is a TRANSCRIPTION of what Core implements today, checked against platform/core/identity/{login.ts, credential-store.ts, credential-verifier.ts, session-credential.ts, pre-auth-admission.ts} and platform/core/http/pre-auth-http.ts. Nothing here is a proposal, a preference or an improvement; where Core and this file disagree, Core is what runs and this file is the defect.

THIS IS NOT AN ACTION CONTRACT AND THESE ARE NOT ACTION SHAPES. Login is a pre-authentication ADMISSION path (docs/decisions/0014 §B): there is no permission, no scope, no ActionContext, no tenant store, no audit row and no Action definition anywhere on it. Reading these shapes as an Action's input and output is the single most likely way to misuse this contract.

ONE CONTRACT SET, TWO CLIENTS. The responsive web client and the Apple client send byte-identical values for the same password and email. That is not a style guideline: the derived value is compared against a stored hash, so a normalisation or KDF divergence between clients means one platform's users cannot log in at all (docs/decisions/0016). TWO NORMALISATIONS ARE IN PLAY AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT — NFC for the password, NFKC plus ASCII-only case folding for the email — and the password half is the one rule here that CORE CANNOT ENFORCE, because Core never receives a password. See derivedKey.

NOT EXECUTED. No JSON Schema implementation exists in this repository (ADR 0009), there is no package.json and no node_modules, and AS1 — the executable form of a Dudo contract — is undecided. These schemas are normative and HAND-CHECKED. No report may describe them as validated. Core's own validation is parsePreAuthBody, which is hand-written and does not read this file.

emailIdentifier.description:
The account identifier the user types. Wire field name: 'email'.

THE CANONICAL DEFINITION IS urn:dudo:schema:account-identifier:1#/$defs/accountIdentifier, added 2026-09-05 after the rule was found restated in five places with no two agreeing. This restatement was one of the CORRECT ones — it already permitted at least one '@', matching Core — and is unchanged in substance. It must stay character-identical to the canonical definition; a divergence is a contract defect.

AND THE LOGIN PATH IS THE ONE THAT WAS ALREADY SAFE: credential-verifier.ts:439 calls isSubmittableIdentifier before normalizeIdentifier at :449. Two other Core paths do not, which is account-identifier-v1's AI-1 — named here so nobody reads that finding as applying to login.

THIS IS DELIBERATELY NOT AN EMAIL VALIDATOR, AND COPYING A STRICTER GRAMMAR INTO A CLIENT WOULD BE A DEFECT. Core's isSubmittableIdentifier (platform/core/identity/credential-store.ts) decides exactly one thing: whether three implementations in three languages will agree on the normalised form. It does not decide whether an address is deliverable — nothing here sends mail — and a stricter grammar would refuse valid addresses for no security gain.

WHAT THIS PATTERN AND THESE BOUNDS TRANSCRIBE, character for character:
  - Length 3 to 254 inclusive. 3 is the shortest thing that can be an address at all ('a@b'). 254 is below RFC 5321's 256-octet path cap, and every byte past it is work an unauthenticated caller can compel on the hashing path.
  - Every character in 0x21..0x7E — printable ASCII. SPACE (0x20) IS EXCLUDED along with the whole control range and everything above 0x7E.
  - At least one '@'. More than one is accepted; Core checks only that one is present.

WHITESPACE IS REFUSED, NEVER TRIMMED, AND THIS IS THE RULE MOST LIKELY TO BE 'HELPFULLY' BROKEN BY A CLIENT. A client that calls trim() before sending has changed the value that becomes the PBKDF2 salt, and the derived key will not match. It is refused rather than trimmed because JavaScript's String.prototype.trim removes the Unicode White_Space set and Swift's trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) removes a different set — so a value that needs trimming is a value the implementations can disagree about. Refusing removes the disagreement instead of arbitrating it.

A VALUE OUTSIDE THESE BOUNDS IS ANSWERED 401 unauthenticated, NOT 400 invalid_argument, as long as it is at most 512 characters. See login-v1.contract.yaml -> errorRulings.theTwoLengthRegimes. That is a real divergence from every Action contract in this repository and it is the shape of Core's actual behaviour, not a wish.

THIS FIELD'S NORMALISATION IS NFKC PLUS ASCII-ONLY CASE FOLDING. THE PASSWORD'S IS NFC ONLY, WITH NO CASE FOLDING AND NO CHARACTER RESTRICTION. The two run on the two inputs of the same PBKDF2 call and are deliberately different; see derivedKey. Applying this field's rule to a password would silently weaken it.

THE ACCEPTED COST, STATED RATHER THAN HIDDEN: AN RFC 6531 INTERNATIONALISED ADDRESS CANNOT LOG IN. A non-ASCII local part, or a non-punycode domain, is refused by the printable-ASCII rule. Punycode domains work, because punycode is ASCII. Relaxing this needs a decision record and shared test vectors for all three implementations, in that order.

derivedKey.description:
The client-side KDF output. Wire field name: 'derived_key'. EXACTLY 43 base64url characters, unpadded — the encoding of 32 bytes.

IT IS NOT THE PASSWORD AND MUST NEVER BE ONE. It is base64url(PBKDF2-SHA256(UTF-8 bytes of NFC(password), salt = UTF-8 bytes of normalizeIdentifier(email), iterations = 600000, length = 32 bytes)). All SIX parameters are NORMATIVE and none is negotiable per client. The full derivation, the per-language equivalents and the reasons are in login-v1.contract.yaml -> clientKdf, which a client author must read before writing either implementation.

THE TWO INPUTS ARE NORMALISED DIFFERENTLY, IN THE SAME THREE LINES OF CLIENT CODE, AND THAT IS THE MOST CONFUSABLE THING IN THIS CONTRACT. The PASSWORD is NFC only — no case folding, no trimming, no character restriction. The EMAIL, which becomes the salt, is validated as printable ASCII, then NFKC, then ASCII-only case folded. NFC for the password and NFKC for the email is deliberate: an identifier is looked up, so collapsing compatibility variants and case is right for it; a password is only ever compared with itself, and every collapse silently removes a distinction the user believed they had chosen — NFKC on a password derives the key of a weaker password than the one that was typed. This is RFC 8265's split between its 'UsernameCaseMapped' and 'OpaqueString' profiles, the latter being what SCRAM and SASL use for exactly this problem. On Apple the two calls differ by one word: precomposedStringWithCanonicalMapping is NFC and is for the password; precomposedStringWithCompatibilityMapping is NFKC and is for the email. Swapping them compiles, runs, and passes any ASCII-only test suite.

ADDED 2026-09-04. docs/decisions/0015 §D originally said only 'the UTF-8 password'; web-agent found the gap while implementing. Without the rule, a non-ASCII password typed in composed and decomposed form is two byte sequences deriving two different keys, so a user enrols on one platform and cannot log in on another — presenting as a wrong password, with no message that could ever say otherwise.

CORE CANNOT ENFORCE THE PASSWORD RULE AND NEVER WILL BE ABLE TO, because Core never receives a password. Every other rule in this contract has a server-side backstop; this one has none, and a wrongly normalised password is indistinguishable from a wrong password to Core, to the logs and to the user. THE ONLY ENFORCEMENT ANYWHERE IN THE PLATFORM IS SHARED TEST VECTORS BINDING BOTH CLIENTS, which makes them a security control rather than a convenience. Do not assume a server check exists.

IT IS A BEARER SECRET IN TRANSIT. Anyone holding this value can log in as the user, exactly as a password would. It is never logged, never stored by a client, never placed in a URL, and never sent anywhere but this endpoint over TLS.

THE WIDTH CHECK IS A MITIGATION AND CORE DOES NOT CLAIM IT IS MORE. docs/decisions/0015 §D records the residual in these terms: a client that posted the raw password instead of the KDF output would be indistinguishable to the server, and requiring exactly 43 base64url characters mitigates but does not close it — a 43-character password drawn from [A-Za-z0-9_-] passes. What actually narrows it today is that enrollment runs Dudo's own tool, which performs the same client-side KDF, so a client sending anything else derives different bytes and is REFUSED. The mismatch fails closed and loud.

A VALUE OF THE WRONG WIDTH OR ALPHABET IS ANSWERED 401 unauthenticated, NOT 400. Core's credential verifier decides it (fromBase64Url at exactly 32 bytes) and every failure on that path is the same fixed refusal.

loginCompleteRequest.description:
The JSON body of POST /auth/login/complete. EXACTLY TWO FIELDS, BOTH REQUIRED, AND NOTHING ELSE IS ACCEPTED.

additionalProperties: false IS ENFORCED BY CORE AND IS NOT ASPIRATIONAL HERE. platform/core/identity/pre-auth-admission.ts::parsePreAuthBody rejects any field the entry point did not declare with invalid_argument and the detail token 'unknown_field', naming the FIELD and never the value. The declared set comes from login.ts's registration and is exactly ['email', 'derived_key'].

SO THERE IS NO organization_id, NO tenant_id, NO remember_me, NO device_name, NO redirect_uri, NO client_id, NO locale AND NO totp FIELD — not undocumented, REJECTED. A caller supplying any of them gets 400 before anything is verified. In particular no Organization hint is accepted at login even though the session issuer supports one: it would make the answer depend on the caller's membership in a named Organization, which is an Organization-membership oracle available to anyone who steals one credential (login.ts).

THREE MORE FLOOR LIMITS APPLY TO THIS BODY, from parsePreAuthBody: at most 4,096 BYTES total, at most 12 fields, and at most 512 characters per string value. Each is answered 400 invalid_argument with a stable detail token ('body_too_large', 'too_many_fields', 'too_long').

TYPES ARE NOT COERCED. Core's floor accepts string, number and boolean primitives and rejects arrays and objects outright ('must_be_a_primitive'), and login.ts then requires BOTH fields to be non-empty STRINGS. So {"email": 12345} passes the floor and is REFUSED 401 by the handler rather than coerced — String(12345) would produce an identifier nobody typed, and coercion on an authentication path is how a type-confusion bug becomes a login bug.

preAuthAcknowledgement.description:
The ONE success body of every pre-authentication endpoint. Rendered from a single constant (platform/core/http/pre-auth-http.ts::PRE_AUTH_ACK_BODY_TEXT), so it is byte-identical across every success on every entry point.

THE SUCCESSFUL LOGIN AND THE 'I DID NOTHING' ACKNOWLEDGEMENT SHARE THIS BODY BYTE FOR BYTE. The only difference between them is the presence of a Set-Cookie header. That is deliberate and it is a disclosure control: a body that varied in length between the two would be a size channel on a path an unauthenticated caller can drive at will.

THERE IS NO TOKEN, NO SESSION IDENTIFIER, NO EXPIRY, NO PRINCIPAL IDENTIFIER, NO ORGANIZATION AND NO USER OBJECT IN THIS BODY, AND NONE MAY BE ADDED. A client that needs the credential reads the Set-Cookie header; see sessionCredential. A client that needs to know who it is asks after authenticating, through the ordinary authenticated path. ADDING ANY FIELD HERE IS BREAKING AND IS ALSO A DISCLOSURE REVIEW, because it reintroduces a body whose length can vary.

status.description: The literal string 'ok'. It is a constant, not a status vocabulary: there is no 'pending', no 'mfa_required' and no 'error' value, and a client must not switch on it. The HTTP status and the presence of Set-Cookie carry everything a client needs.

sessionCredential.description:
The session credential, delivered ONLY in the Set-Cookie header of a successful login. It is not in the response body and never will be.

IT IS OPAQUE TO EVERY CLIENT. Deliberately no pattern and no maximum here: a client must not parse it, split it, validate its shape, decode any part of it, or infer anything from its length. Core's current format is <session_id>.<truncated HMAC> (docs/decisions/0015 §A), and A CLIENT THAT DEPENDS ON THAT HAS BOUND ITSELF TO AN IMPLEMENTATION DETAIL THAT MAY CHANGE WITHOUT A CONTRACT CHANGE. It carries no claims — no organization, no principal, no expiry, no scope. It is not a JWT and must never be treated as one; everything about the session is read from the session row on every request, which is what makes revoking a membership take effect immediately rather than at expiry.

HOW IT IS DELIVERED. Exactly one Set-Cookie header:
    dudo_session=<value>; Max-Age=43200; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
All five attributes are forced by the transport (platform/core/http/pre-auth-http.ts) and are not negotiable, not per-client, and not configurable. Max-Age is 43,200 seconds — twelve hours — derived from one constant shared with the session row's expiry so a cookie cannot outlive its row.

ONE VALUE, TWO CARRIERS. The web client lets the browser hold the cookie and sends nothing explicitly. The Apple client may read the value from Set-Cookie (or let URLSession's cookie store hold it) and present it on later requests as 'Authorization: Bearer <value>'. THE DIRECTION IS ONE-WAY: the cookie is the source and the bearer header is a carrier for it. HttpOnly means page JavaScript cannot read it, so a web client cannot construct the bearer form and must not try.

A REQUEST CARRYING BOTH CARRIERS WITH DIFFERENT VALUES IS REFUSED unauthenticated, never resolved by precedence — picking a winner is how a cookie an attacker plants cross-site beats a header the application set. Identical values in both are accepted.
